references.text: Describes intentional killing with malicious intent, where the murderer must die - the same principle of premeditated murder as in Exodus 21:14
Prohibits accepting ransom for a murderer's life; the murderer must die - emphasizing the seriousness of intentional killing
About a man who hates his neighbor and lies in wait for him and kills him - parallel to killing with deceit (בְעָרְמָה)
Adonija grabs hold of the horns of the altar to seek refuge, but Solomon lets him go conditionally - illustrating the principle of the altar as a place of refuge
Joab flees to the tent of the Lord and grabs the horns of the altar, but is killed there because of his crimes - direct application of taking the murderer away from the altar
Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed - fundamental principle of capital punishment for murder
Whoever strikes a person down must die - confirming the death penalty for killing
Describes evil people who plan wicked deeds and are quick to shed blood - evil and deceit in murder plots
Both verses establish the principle that certain serious crimes against fellow humans require capital punishment to cleanse society.
Numbers 35:20 gives the concrete definition of 'killing with deceit' mentioned in Exodus 21:14.
Complementary verses: Exodus regulates refuge before execution, while Deuteronomy regulates the carrying out and visibility of the punishment afterward.
Contrast reference: Exodus states that the murderer must be removed from the altar, while 1 Samuel warns that certain sins (here involving priests) will still not be removed as punishment.
Thematic parallel about 'deceit' as a tool for evil that is inevitably exposed and punished.
